common_name: AU-Leader Chestnut (Auburn University Precocious Chinese Chestnut)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; AU-Leader was released by Auburn University alongside AU-Cropper and AU-Homestead from the same Deep South-adapted breeding population, and needs a second, genetically distinct chestnut cultivar nearby for full cross-pollination.

directions: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. AU-Leader is a Chinese chestnut selection from Auburn University's chestnut improvement program, drawn from the same precocious, blight-resistant seedling population that also produced AU-Cropper and AU-Homestead, and was chosen for a strongly upright, single-leader growth habit that makes it easier to train and maintain than the sprawling form typical of many chestnut selections. Like its sibling releases it inherits good resistance to chestnut blight and begins bearing at a young age on a grafted tree. Nuts run large for a Chinese chestnut, averaging roughly a dozen grams each, and mature and drop free of the split burr in early-to-mid September, ahead of many other Southern-adapted cultivars. Space trees widely to accommodate a broad mature canopy, and interplant with a second unrelated chestnut cultivar within pollination range for a full nut set.

common_name: AU Buck IV Chestnut (Auburn University Annual-Bearing Chinese Chestnut)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; AU Buck IV is an open-pollinated selection out of AU-Cropper, bred for the heat and humidity of Alabama and the wider Gulf South, and needs a second, genetically distinct chestnut cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. AU Buck IV is part of a numbered series (AU Buck I through V) of Chinese chestnut selections patented by Auburn University from open-pollinated seedlings of the AU-Cropper cultivar, chosen for blight resistance, precocious bearing, and dependable annual cropping rather than the alternate-bearing pattern common in seedling chestnut trees. It sets a medium to heavy crop of large nuts most years once established, and like other Auburn chestnut releases it is bred specifically to perform under the heat, humidity, and soilborne disease pressure of the Deep South. Space trees widely for a broad mature canopy and good air circulation, and plant a second unrelated Chinese chestnut cultivar nearby, since chestnuts are not reliably self-fruitful. Harvest nuts from the ground in September-October as the spiny burrs split open, and refrigerate cured nuts to sweeten the starches before eating.
sources: Auburn University College of Agriculture — Chestnut Growers Information
US Plant Patent PP20624 — Chestnut plant named AU BUCK IV

common_name: GA-866 Jujube (USDA Chico Sweet Crisp Jujube)

planting.note: Plant grafted tree in spring in full sun in any well-drained soil; GA-866 is a partially self-fruitful jujube from the USDA's mid-20th-century Chico, California breeding program and sets a heavier crop with a Li or Lang jujube nearby for cross-pollination; fruit ripens mid-to-late September, about the same time as Lang.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; jujube tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil far better than most fruit trees once established, and thrives in the long, hot Gulf Coast growing season. GA-866 originated at the USDA Plant Introduction Station in Chico, California, from an unrecorded cross evaluated during the agency's mid-1900s jujube trials, and was never given a formal cultivar name before the breeding program was discontinued — growers and nurseries have since propagated and sold it simply under its USDA accession number. The fruit is elongated and plump, ripening to a shiny reddish-brown skin with dense, crisp, apple-like flesh and a concentrated sweetness that many growers rate among the best-flavored jujubes for fresh eating. Compared with the more common Li and Lang cultivars it remains relatively rare in commerce, but it is valued for strong drought and cold tolerance, high yields, and good disease resistance. Space trees to allow for their naturally upright, somewhat thorny, suckering growth habit, and remove root suckers as needed to keep the planting in bounds.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Chico Plant Introduction Station jujube trials

planting.note: Plant grafted tree in spring in full to partial sun in well-drained soil; Vista White is prized for its unusually sweet, pale, sherbet-like flesh, distinct from the more common orange-fleshed loquat cultivars, and performs well in zones 8-10, though a run of hard freezes below the upper 20s F during bloom or fruit set can reduce or eliminate the crop for the year.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; loquats tolerate poor soils and short dry spells once established but size and flavor improve with regular moisture during fruit development; thin heavy clusters for larger fruit and harvest when fully colored and slightly soft, since loquats do not continue ripening after picking. Vista White is a California-selected loquat grown mainly by home orchardists and specialty growers for its distinctive creamy white to pale-yellow flesh, a marked contrast to the orange flesh of widely grown cultivars like Premier and Big Jim. The round, light-yellow fruits hang in grape-like clusters of fifteen to twenty and have a delicate, very sweet, almost sherbet-like flavor with mild tang, making them popular for fresh eating. Trees bloom in fall and ripen fruit in late winter to spring, ahead of most other tree fruit, and tolerate periods of drought and a range of soil types once established as long as drainage is good and soil salinity is low. As with all loquats, the open flowers and developing fruit are more cold-sensitive than the tree itself, so a sheltered, south-facing planting site improves crop reliability in zone 8-9 gardens near the cooler edge of the loquat's range.

planting.note: Plant grafted, self-fertile tree in spring in full to partial sun in compost-rich, well-drained soil; MacBeth is a late-season loquat noted for exceptionally large, richly flavored fruit and is well suited to zones 8-10, including the Gulf Coast, given a sheltered site protected from hard freezes during bloom.

directions: Plant in compost-rich, well-drained loam in full to partial sun; MacBeth is self-fertile and does not require a second loquat for fruit set, though nearby trees can improve yield. The tree has a handsome, symmetrical growth habit and can reach around 20-30 feet at full maturity if left untrained, so prune annually to keep fruit within easy reach in a home orchard. MacBeth ripens later than early cultivars like Gold Nugget and produces exceptionally large, orange-skinned fruit with creamy flesh that balances sweetness and acidity, often compared to notes of plum; the size and flavor have made it one of the most sought-after loquat cultivars among backyard growers and collectors. Like other loquats, MacBeth blooms in fall and ripens fruit in late winter to spring, and open flowers and young fruit are more cold-tender than the mature tree, so a warm, sheltered planting site near a south-facing wall improves crop reliability at the cooler edge of its range.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Eriobotrya japonica Plant Toolbox

common_name: Prilop Pecan (Historic Scab-Resistant Texas Native Pecan)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant (January-February in zone 9) in deep, well-drained soil; Prilop is a native-type Texas selection valued mainly for its strong scab resistance in humid regions, and benefits from a second, genetically distinct pecan cultivar nearby for reliable cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible cross-pollinating cultivar nearby. Prilop originated as a native pecan seedling growing along the Lavaca River south of Halletsville in Lavaca County, Texas, and was propagated and preserved by grafters after the original tree was destroyed in a 1940 flood; it is sometimes also found under the names Steffek or Kallus after growers who helped keep the selection in circulation before wood was sent to the USDA-ARS pecan collection. Like many Texas native-type selections, Prilop produces a smaller nut than large modern commercial cultivars but is notably scab-resistant, an important trait for low-spray home orchards in the humid Gulf South, and it was recognized as a Texas Pecan Show state champion native selection. It remains a solid, low-maintenance choice for East Texas and similar Gulf Coast growing conditions, though it is generally considered less productive overall than higher-yielding modern releases like Caddo or Oconee. Correct zinc deficiency with a spring foliar zinc spray and water deeply during nut fill in late summer for the best kernel development.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — National Clonal Germplasm Repository, Pecan Cultivars
